segments.text: section 4. You are going to listen to a lecture on the topic of cerebral palsy.
First you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully
and answer questions 31 to 40. Today I'm going to talk about the most common
modes of disability in childhood, cerebral palsy or CP. In medical terms,
terms, cerebral, means relating to the brain and palsy means weakness or problems with
using the muscles. So, in fact, it's not solely a disease, but a group of disorders
that affect our ability to move and maintain balance and posture.
In the US, 3 in 1,000 children have cerebral palsy according to the Centers for Disease
control and prevention, the CDC. The condition is more common in boys than in girls.
What causes CP in the first place? Cerebral palsy, CP, is caused by abnormal development
of the brain or damage to the developing brain that affects a child's ability to control
his or her muscles. There are several possible causes of the abnormal development or damage.
People used to think that CP was mainly caused by lack of oxygen during the birth process.
Now scientists think that this causes only a small number of CP cases.
According to the National Institutes of Neurological Disorders and Strokes,
the main causes of cerebral palsy during pregnancy, birth and infancy include first, infections.
Infections can happen during pregnancy or after birth.
birth. Second is problems with blood flow to the brain such as a stroke or bleeding
in the brain associated with a blood clotting problem. The last one is injuries which are
often head injuries from vehicle accidents. The brain damage that leads to CP can happen
before birth, during birth, within a month after birth, or during the first years of
a child's life while the brain is still developing.
Based on the time the damage occurs, we can divide CP into two types. Congenital CP and
acquired CP. The majority of CP cases around 90% are congenital which means the brain damage
happens before or during birth. The causes for this type of CP are largely unknown but
scientists have figured out some factors that may put a baby in risk of congenital CP.
The first one is low birth weight. Children who weigh less than 2.5 kilograms at birth,
especially those who weigh less than 1.5 kilograms, have a greater chance of having CP.
Then we have premature birth. Children who are born before the 37th week of pregnancy,
especially if they were born before the 32nd week of pregnancy, have a greater chance of
having CP. Some other common risk factors are multiple births, infection during pregnancy
and birth complications. A small percentage of CP is caused by brain damage that occurs
more than 28 days after birth. This is called acquired CP and usually is
associated with an infection such as meningitis or head injury. If we look at
the areas of the brain that are affected we can separate CP into three
different types spastic, dyskinetic and ataxic. Spastic CP is the most common
type of CP. It accounts for about 80% of people with CP. Spastic CP patients have increased
muscle tone. This means their muscles are stiff and, as a result, their movements can
be awkward. There are three types of spastic CP, classified by what parts of the body are
affected. The first type of spastic CP is spastic
diplegia. In this type of CP, muscle stiffness is mainly in the legs with the
arms less affected or not affected at all. People with spastic diplegia might
have difficulty walking because tight hip and leg muscles cause their legs to
pulled together turn inwards and cross at the knees also known as scissoring.
The second one is spastic hemiplegia. This type of CP affects only one side of
a person's body usually the arm which is more effective than the leg. The last
and also the most severe form of spastic CP is spastic quadriplegia. It affects
all four limbs, the trunk and the face. People with spastic quadriplegia usually
cannot walk and often have other developmental disabilities such as
intellectual disabilities, seizures or problems with vision, hearing or speech.
The second type of CP after spastic is dyskinetic. People with dyskinetic CP
have problems controlling the movement of their hands, arms, feet and legs, making it
difficult to sit and walk. The movements are uncontrollable and can be slow and
writhing or rapid and jerky. Sometimes the face and tongue are affected and the
person has a hard time sucking, swallowing and talking. A person with
dyskinetic CP has muscle tone that can change varying from too tight to loose
not only from day to day but even during a single day. The last type of CP is
ataxic CP. People with ataxic CP have problems with balance and coordination.
They might be unsteady when they walk.
They might have a hard time with quick movements or movements that need a lot of control, like
writing.
They might have a hard time controlling their hands or arms when they reach for something.
